excerpt.locator: La Corona, seven sonnets, Holy Sonnets; complete individual work; opens “1. DEIGNE at my hands this crown of prayer and praise, Weav'd in my low devout…”; closes “…thy holy Spirit, my Muse did raise, Deigne at my hands this crowne of prayer and praise.”.

questions.prompt: The first sonnet sets two crowns against each other. What are they, and which one does the poet ask for?
facilitatorNotes: Not the “vile crowne of fraile bayes,” the laurel of literary fame, but what Christ’s “thorny crowne” won: “A crowne of Glory, which doth flower alwayes.” The sequence itself is a crown he offers. “The ends crowne our workes, but thou crown’st our ends” plays on ends as aims and as deaths.
evidence: But doe not, with a vile crowne of fraile bayes, Reward my muses white sincerity,
But what thy thorny crowne gain'd, that give mee,
The ends crowne our workes, but thou crown'st our ends,

questions.prompt: “Annunciation” is built on paradoxes. Choose two and explain them.
facilitatorNotes: God who cannot sin bears all sins and, unable to die, must die; Mary is “Thy Makers maker, and thy Fathers mother,” because the God who made her is born from her. “Immensity cloysterd in thy deare wombe” compresses the incarnation into one line: the infinite enclosed in the small. The paradoxes are Donne’s way of saying something that ordinary logic cannot.
evidence: Which cannot sinne, and yet all sinnes must beare, Which cannot die, yet cannot chuse but die,
Thy Makers maker, and thy Fathers mother;
Immensity cloysterd in thy deare wombe.

questions.prompt: In “Nativitie” and “Temple” the speaker speaks to his own soul and to Joseph. Why enter the scenes himself instead of describing them?
facilitatorNotes: He asks his soul to look “with thy faiths eyes,” to kiss the child and go with him into Egypt, and he tells Joseph to turn back and find the boy among the Doctors. This is meditation as imagined presence: the reader too is placed in the scene. The paradox that God “would have need to be pittied by thee” makes pity the soul’s response.
evidence: Seest thou, my Soule, with thy faiths eyes, how he Which fils all place, yet none holds him, doth lye?
Was not his pity towards thee wondrous high, That would have need to be pittied by thee?
Ioseph turne backe; see where your child doth sit,

questions.prompt: Where does the sequence turn from Christ’s story to the speaker’s need, and how does the last sonnet close the circle?
facilitatorNotes: At the crucifixion: “Now thou art lifted up, draw mee to thee,” and the linking line asks one drop of blood to moisten his “dry soule,” which the next sonnet turns into a promise of rising. The last sonnet names Christ Ramme, Lambe and Torch and ends on the first line again, so the crown closes as the prayer is offered. Readers may find the linking satisfying or mechanical; either can be argued from the joins.
evidence: Now thou art lifted up, draw mee to thee,
Moyst, with one drop of thy blood, my dry soule.
Deigne at my hands this crowne of prayer and praise.

readings.title: A Hymne to Christ, at the Authors last going into Germany
readings.challenge: Notice everything the speaker gives up, and the images of sea, storm and darkness he chooses.
readings.focus: A farewell to everyone he loves, turned into a marriage to God.
readings.context: Donne, by then a priest, wrote this before sailing to Germany in 1619 with an English embassy, unsure that he would return. An embleme is a picture with a moral meaning; the Arke is Noah’s ark, which carried its passengers safely through the Flood; a bill of Divorce is a written decree ending a marriage.

excerpt.locator: A Hymne to Christ, at the Authors last going into Germany, Divine Poems; complete individual work; opens “IN what torne ship soever I embarke, That ship shall be my embleme of thy Arke; What sea…”; closes “…God only, I goe out of sight: And to scape stormy dayes, I chuse An Everlasting night.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza turn a dangerous voyage into a sign of faith?
facilitatorNotes: Whatever torn ship carries him becomes an emblem of the Ark, and whatever sea drowns him an emblem of Christ’s blood. God’s anger is a mask, and behind it are eyes that “never will despise.” The danger is not denied; it is reread.
evidence: That ship shall be my embleme of thy Arke;
What sea soever swallow mee, that flood Shall be to mee an embleme of thy blood;
Thy face; yet through that maske I know those eyes,

questions.prompt: What does he “sacrifice” in the second stanza, and how does the image of sap in winter explain his going?
facilitatorNotes: England and everyone he loves. As he puts seas between himself and them, he asks God to put a sea between his sins and God. Sap draws down to the root in winter; in his own winter he goes where only God, “th’Eternall root Of true Love,” can be known. The voyage becomes a withdrawal inward.
evidence: I sacrifice this Iland unto thee, And all whom I lov'd there, and who lov'd mee;
Put thou thy sea betwixt my sinnes and thee.
As the trees sap doth seeke the root below In winter,

questions.prompt: The third stanza wants God to be jealous. Why? Explain “O, if thou car’st not whom I love Alas, thou lov’st not mee.”
facilitatorNotes: Religion does not forbid a loving nature, “The amorousnesse of an harmonious Soule,” but God wants that love for himself. A God indifferent to whom he loves would not be loving him at all, so jealousy is proof of love. The language is a lover’s, which suits the poet of the Songs and Sonets.
evidence: Nor thou nor thy religion dost controule, The amorousnesse of an harmonious Soule,
As thou Art jealous, Lord, so I am jealous now,
O, if thou car'st not whom I love Alas, thou lov'st not mee.

questions.prompt: The poem ends, “I chuse An Everlasting night.” Is that an image of death, of devotion, or both? Look at the line about churches.
facilitatorNotes: He divorces himself from Fame, Wit and Hopes, “false mistresses,” and is married to God. Churches are best for prayer when darkest, and he goes “out of sight” to see God only: darkness as concentration. But the everlasting night is also death, which he half expects on this voyage. Readers can hear the ending as serene or as bleak.
evidence: Seale then this bill of my Divorce to All,
Churches are best for Prayer, that have least light:
And to scape stormy dayes, I chuse An Everlasting night.
